The case for dismantling the Federal Reserve and ending fiat money is not a nostalgic yearning for a bygone era, but a moral and economic imperative to restore true prosperity, individual liberty, and financial integrity. For over a century, the Federal Reserve’s monopoly on money has been an engine of silent confiscation, cyclical destruction, and entrenched privilege. The only durable remedy is to abolish central banking entirely and replace it with a system grounded in sound money—either through a classical gold standard or, more robustly, through a regime of free banking in which competing private currencies emerge and thrive.

The central evil of a central bank is its power to conjure money from nothing. The Federal Reserve, like all fiat institutions, creates currency ex nihilo, debasing the value of every dollar already held by savers and wage earners. This is not a bug; it is the defining feature. The dollar has lost over 97% of its purchasing power since 1913. Inflation is a regressive tax that falls hardest on the poor, the elderly, and anyone irresponsible enough to hold cash rather than speculate on assets that float upward on the rising tide of liquidity. To call this a “standard of living” improvement is a statistical illusion; real wage growth for ordinary workers tracks not abundance but the silent theft of their savings. Ending the Fed and returning to a gold standard would strip away the state’s ability to engineer this hidden expropriation, tying currency issuance to a real, costly commodity that no committee can fabricate in a boardroom.

Beyond the steady erosion of purchasing power, the Fed’s manipulation of interest rates is the root cause of the violent boom-bust cycle that has massacred economies since its inception. By artificially lowering rates below their market-determined level, the central bank sends a false signal to entrepreneurs and investors, triggering a malinvestment boom—housing in 2008, tech in the dot-com crash, and countless infrastructure follies before that. The inevitable bust is then blamed on capitalism, when it is precisely the government’s interference with the price of money that is the culprit. A gold standard or a free banking system eliminates this plague by making the rate of interest a genuine market price reflecting the actual supply of savings. In a free banking system, competitive note-issuing banks must maintain convertibility into a base money (which could be gold) and clear each other’s notes through a private clearinghouse. Any bank that over-issues will rapidly face adverse clearings and a draining of its reserves, forcing immediate discipline. Thus, credit expansion cannot become systemic, and the cycle is strangled at birth.

The Federal Reserve is also the indispensable patron of big government, Wall Street, and the warfare state. Without the ability to monetize debt through open market operations, the federal government would be forced to confront spending with the immediate friction of taxation or genuine borrowing from real savers. Trillion-dollar deficits, endless foreign interventions, and bailouts for “too-big-to-fail” institutions are funded on the back of the Fed’s printing press. Abolishing the Fed and adopting a gold standard would sever the unholy umbilical cord connecting the state to the money supply, revitalizing the constitutional requirement that public money be coined and its value regulated by a metal, not a board of governors. It would force a fiscal sanity that is otherwise politically impossible, shrinking Leviathan to a scale compatible with liberty.

Critics of the gold standard often point to the supposed “straitjacket” it imposes on economic growth, claiming that a rigid money supply cannot accommodate a growing economy. This is a misunderstanding of history and economics. Under a gold standard, the supply of money does increase as mining and technology improve, but incrementally and predictably, not by fiat decree. More importantly, the key role of money is not to expand with every whim of appetite but to serve as a stable unit of account and store of value. A free banking system with competing currencies provides the ideal evolutionary flexibility: banks can issue notes and digital claims fully convertible into a base asset like gold. The market, not a monopoly central planner, would then determine which monetary instruments best maintain their value. History shows that in such environments, citizens migrate toward the most trustworthy currencies, forcing banks to maintain high reserves and spotless reputations. The “money supply” becomes a bottom-up phenomenon, governed by the solemn contract between issuer and user, not a macroeconomic lever for politicians.

The alternative of a gold standard, while vastly superior to fiat, is often criticized for being a “barbarous relic” subject to the vagaries of mining. But the free banking model escapes this critique entirely by detaching the definition of base money from a single commodity, if society so chooses. In a genuinely free market, people could use gold, silver, or even mathematically auditable cryptocurrencies as their base of convertibility. The crucial difference from our current system is not the specific metal but the absence of a legal tender mandate and a central monetary authority. Competition in currency would do for money what the end of state churches did for religion: produce a richer, more honest, and more resilient ecosystem of trust. The state would only enforce contracts against fraud, not dictate what counts as legal tender.

The current system is held up by a mountain of myths and a wall of vested interests. We are told that a central bank is necessary to be a “lender of last resort” in a panic. Yet panics themselves are overwhelmingly the children of prior credit expansion. Without a central bank to underwrite universal moral hazard, private clearinghouses in a free banking system organized liquidity support through cooperation without socializing losses. We are told that discretionary monetary policy can steer the economy toward full employment, but this is the height of intellectual hubris. The performance of the Fed over the last two decades—fueling serial bubbles, ignoring the warning signs of 2008, then unleashing unprecedented asset purchases that enriched the few and immiserated the many—reads as a confession of incompetence, not a case for more power.

The path forward requires an act of legislative abolition, not reform. The Federal Reserve Act must be repealed. Legal tender laws, which compel acceptance of depreciating Federal Reserve notes, must be rescinded. The government’s own dollar holdings, as well as the Treasury’s gold reserves, should back a transition to a redeemable currency, with citizens free to use whatever monetary instruments they wish thereafter—be they gold coins, silver certificates, bank-issued digital notes convertible into gold, or private cryptographic tokens. The market, left unmolested, will rapidly discover the most dependable media of exchange, and the long night of inflationary theft and central planning will end.

Abolishing the Fed and returning to sound, competitive money is not a dream of anarchic fantasy; it is the reassertion of a simple truth: that money is a tool of voluntary human cooperation, not a weapon of state coercion. It would restore the link between effort and reward, protect the widow’s mite from slow-motion confiscation, and dismantle the machinery that finances unnecessary wars and corporate welfare. The choice is stark: we can continue to worship the green paper deities of a fiat pantheon, marching toward the currency crises that have devoured every paper empire in history, or we can summon the courage to build a monetary system worthy of a free people, where money is as honest as the work that earns it.

Core Reasons for Abolishing the Federal Reserve and Fiat Money

1. The Inflationary Bias of Central Banking Proponents argue that a central bank with a monopoly on currency issuance possesses an irresistible incentive to expand the money supply. Because government spending is politically popular and taxation is politically painful, the state relies on the Federal Reserve to purchase its debt with newly created money. This monetization of deficits dilutes the existing stock of money, leading to a sustained rise in the price level. By pushing rates below the market-clearing level, the Fed induces malinvestment: entrepreneurs are misled into believing that society has saved more than it actually has, launching long-term capital projects that are unsustainable. The inevitable correction materializes as a boom-bust cycle. 4. Erosion of Purchasing Power and Economic Disenfranchisement Fiat money is decried as a mechanism for systematic decapitalization. Since its creation requires no sacrifice of real resources, it is “easy money” that relentlessly depreciates. Workers must negotiate nominal wage increases simply to keep pace with the money-printing they did not authorize, while those on fixed incomes or with savings in bank deposits watch their purchasing power evaporate. The arrangement is viewed as an institutionalized fraud that benefits debtors and the state at the expense of creditors and ordinary citizens.

5. Central Planning Hubris The Federal Reserve’s dual mandate—to achieve both price stability and maximum employment—is seen as a textbook case of the knowledge problem identified by F.A. Hayek. Proponents of abolition contend that no committee of economists can possibly possess the granular, dispersed information needed to set the “correct” quantity of money or the appropriate interest rate across an entire economy. The attempt to do so turns monetary policy into a series of experimental interventions, with millions of people serving as unwitting guinea pigs.

Supposed Benefits of Adopting a Gold Standard

For those favouring a gold standard, the metal’s key virtue is that its supply is governed by the costly, real-world process of mining rather than the discretion of central bankers. The expected benefits are:

1. Long-Run Price Stability Under a classical gold standard, the general price level was roughly stable over long stretches of time, with periods of mild inflation during gold discoveries offset by mild deflation during productivity gains. This removes the constant upward drift in prices that has been the norm since 1971. Businesses can plan for the future without having to insure against monetary debasement, and the real value of savings is preserved across generations.

2. Fiscal Discipline on Government A gold anchor functions as a straitjacket on state spending. Governments cannot run persistent deficits and have the central bank monetize the resulting debt, because an outflow of gold would punish such profligacy. The gold standard thus directly restricts the state’s ability to finance wars, welfare expansions, or other politically motivated projects through inflation, forcing a greater reliance on transparent taxation or genuine borrowing from voluntary savers.

3. Elimination of the Business Cycle Proponents from the Austrian School argue that a commodity money with inelastic supply would prevent the artificial lowering of interest rates that causes malinvestment. With money that cannot be created out of thin air, banks’ credit expansion is limited to the pool of real savings. This would, in theory, synchronize the structure of production with consumers’ true time preferences, eliminating the cyclical pattern of boom and bust entirely.

4. Trust Through Tangibility A metallic standard provides a transparent, apolitical monetary base that individuals can verify. The psychological and practical benefits of a money that is not someone else’s liability—and that has no counterparty risk—are considered foundational for long-term confidence. International trade would also be simplified, as gold has historically served as a global unit of account, reducing exchange-rate uncertainty and currency manipulation between nations.

Supposed Benefits of a Free Market in Currencies

An alternative reform platform, associated with thinkers like F.A. Hayek in his later work Denationalisation of Money, goes beyond the gold standard and advocates the complete abolition of government’s monetary monopoly. In this vision, private entities would issue their own currencies, and the market would select those that hold their value best. The expected benefits are:

1. Monetary Competition Breeds Quality Just as competition improves the quality of any good or service, it would force currency issuers to maintain stable purchasing power to attract users. Any issuer that inflated its currency would find its customers rapidly switching to a more reliable competitor. The survival of a currency would depend on the issuer’s credibility, not legal tender laws or the coercive power of the state.

2. End of Inflation as a Policy Tool With no single issuer capable of imposing its currency on an entire economy, the capacity to engineer systematic inflation would vanish. The government itself would have to borrow in a currency that the market trusts, meaning it could no longer debase its way out of debt. Inflationary monetary policy would be disciplined by the immediate threat of currency substitution.

3. Discovery of an Optimal Medium of Exchange The market process would reveal which characteristics—be it a fixed quantity, a basket of commodities, or an algorithmic rule—best serve as a stable store of value and unit of account. The chosen currency or currencies would not be imposed by fiat but would emerge spontaneously from the voluntary choices of millions of individuals. This resolves Hayek’s knowledge problem: no one needs to know the “right” amount of money; the competitive process discovers it.

4. Financial System Resilience A multi-currency regime would inherently decentralize risk. A crisis of confidence in one issuer would not trigger a systemic meltdown requiring a central bank bailout because the failing currency would be quarantined by the market. Depositors would have a direct incentive to monitor the health of their currency issuers, restoring the market discipline that central banking has eroded.

In sum, the proponents of these alternatives share a common conviction: that money is not a creature of the state but a social institution best left to either the impersonal discipline of nature (gold) or the demanding test of competitive enterprise (free banking). Abolishing the Federal Reserve and fiat money is therefore cast as a liberation—freeing citizens from a silent tax, economies from disruptive cycles, and governments from temptations that corrupt the very foundations of exchange.

The Federal Reserve System, established in 1913, stands as a monument to centralized economic control and the abandonment of sound monetary principles. Returning to a gold standard offers a powerful antidote. A gold standard imposes discipline: government spending must be financed through taxation or borrowing in the open market, not by printing money. This naturally limits the size and scope of government. It provides a stable, long-term store of value, protecting savings and encouraging long-term investment over speculation. While critics point to historical episodes of deflation under gold, this was often a benign consequence of productivity gains, making goods cheaper for everyone. Free banking systems in Scotland (1716-1845) and Canada (1817-1914) demonstrated remarkable resilience, innovation, and stability without central banks, operating through market-based clearinghouses and mutual support mechanisms during crises. The "lender of last resort" argument is fundamentally flawed; it merely institutionalizes moral hazard and encourages the very recklessness it purports to prevent. True stability comes from sound money, market discipline, and the absence of bailout guarantees.

Abolishing the Federal Reserve, ending fiat currency, and embracing sound money – whether through gold or free banking – is not a backward step. It is a leap forward into a future of economic liberty, personal financial security, and sustainable growth. It dismantles an engine of inflation, inequality, and cyclical devastation. It strips government of its most insidious tool for stealthy expansion. It restores accountability, placing control over money back into the hands of the people through market choice rather than in the hands of unaccountable central planners. Introduction

The Federal Reserve System, established in 1913, has long been a contentious issue in American politics and economics. The Federal Reserve's Monopoly on Money Creation

The Federal Reserve, as the central bank of the United States, holds a monopoly on money creation. This power is exercised through its control over the money supply and interest rates. However, this monopoly is problematic for several reasons.

Firstly, it concentrates power in the hands of a few individuals, the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Open Market Committee, who make decisions that significantly impact the economy. This lack of checks and balances can lead to poor decision-making, as history has shown with the Fed's role in the 2008 financial crisis.

Secondly, the Fed's control over the money supply enables it to engage in quantitative easing, effectively printing money to stimulate the economy. While this policy can provide short-term benefits, it also leads to inflation, which disproportionately affects the poor and middle class. Furthermore, it distorts market signals, leading to misallocation of resources and encouraging excessive risk-taking.

The Fiat Currency Problem

The Federal Reserve's actions are facilitated by the use of fiat currency, a currency that has no intrinsic value and is not backed by a physical commodity. The value of fiat currency is determined by supply and demand, and the Fed's control over supply makes it a powerful tool for manipulation.

Fiat currency allows for excessive government spending and debt accumulation, as the government can always print more money to meet its obligations. This leads to a moral hazard, where the government is incentivized to spend beyond its means, leading to inflation and economic instability.

Moreover, fiat currency is vulnerable to loss of confidence, as seen in countries like Zimbabwe and Venezuela. When people lose faith in a currency, it can lead to hyperinflation and economic collapse. A gold standard or free banking system would mitigate this risk, as the currency's value would be backed by a physical commodity or market demand.

The Gold Standard and Free Banking: Historical Precedent and Theoretical Advantages

Historical evidence and economic theory both support the advantages of a gold standard or free banking system.

  1. The Gold Standard: The gold standard, where the currency is backed by a fixed amount of gold, was used by many countries in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It promoted economic stability, as the supply of money was tied to the supply of gold, limiting the ability of governments to print money. It also facilitated international trade, as the value of currencies was fixed relative to each other. Critics argue that the gold standard can lead to deflation and economic stagnation, but this can be mitigated by allowing for some flexibility in the gold backing.

  2. Free Banking: Free banking, a system where private banks issue their own currency, was used in the United States before the Civil War. It promoted competition among banks, leading to lower fees and better service for customers. It also limited the ability of governments to manipulate the money supply, as banks would only issue currency backed by gold or other commodities. Critics argue that free banking can lead to bank runs and economic instability, but these risks can be mitigated through proper regulation and insurance.

Conclusion

The Federal Reserve's monopoly on money creation, facilitated by the use of fiat currency, leads to economic instability, concentrates power in the hands of unelected officials, and enables excessive government spending. A return to a gold standard or free banking system would mitigate these risks, promoting economic stability, limiting government intervention, and enhancing individual liberty.

Critics may argue that these systems are outdated or impractical, but the historical evidence and economic theory support their advantages. Moreover, the status quo is not without its risks, as the 2008 financial crisis and the ongoing debate over inflation demonstrate.

In conclusion, the case for abolishing the Federal Reserve and returning to a gold standard or free banking system is strong. It is a matter of promoting economic stability, limiting government intervention, and enhancing individual liberty. The time has come to reconsider our approach to money and banking, and to embrace a system that puts power back in the hands of the people.

The Constitution grants Congress the power to coin money and regulate its value, not to delegate this authority to an independent central bank. The Federal Reserve, with its unusual hybrid public-private structure, operates with remarkable independence from both Congress and the executive branch, raising fundamental questions about democratic accountability. When an unelected body controls the most powerful lever of economic policy—the supply of money—who truly governs the nation?

Sound money has historically been understood as money whose value is determined by the market rather than by government decree. The current system represents a radical departure from millennia of monetary history, wherein gold and silver served as natural, market-chosen monies. The philosophical case for ending central banking rests on the principle that individuals should have the right to use whatever money they trust, rather than having currency imposed by government mandate backed by legal tender laws.

The Economic Case Against Fiat Currency

Fiat currency—money declared legal tender by government decree without intrinsic value—creates structural incentives for monetary manipulation. The Federal Reserve's dual mandate to promote maximum employment and price stability gives it both the motive and the means to inflate the money supply beyond what sound economic principles would dictate. History demonstrates that governments consistently succumb to the temptation of printing money to fund spending, satisfy political demands, or delay economic corrections.

The hidden tax of inflation disproportionately harms those least able to protect themselves: workers on fixed wages, saversAccumulating wealth through labor, and those on fixed incomes. Meanwhile, those closest to the newly created money—financial institutions and the government itself—benefit at the expense of ordinary citizens. This represents a form of wealth redistribution that occurs without legislative debate or democratic consent.

The manipulation of interest rates through Federal Reserve policy distorts capital allocation, creating malinvestments that must eventually be liquidated in recessions. The Austrian school of economics has long argued that artificial booms driven by easy credit lead inevitably to busts. The 2008 financial crisis and the subsequent "recovery" that saw asset prices soar while wages stagnated for most workers seems to validate this critique.

The Case for the Gold Standard

Proponents of the gold standard argue that tying currency to a tangible commodity imposes financial discipline that politicians and central bankers cannot be trusted to exercise themselves. Under a gold standard, the money supply expands only as gold mining makes new gold available, preventing the government from financing deficits through inflation. Historical evidence suggests that the gold standard era featured generally stable prices over the long run, though with periods of deflation.

Critics argue that the gold standard limits monetary policy flexibility. However, this limitation might be better understood as a feature rather than a bug. The inability to inflate currency would force governments to balance budgets, making fiscal discipline a requirement rather than a choice. Furthermore, the gold standard would eliminate the boom-bust cycle by preventing the artificial expansion of credit that precedes economic crises.

International monetary stability characterized the pre-World War I gold standard, as exchange rates remained fixed and predictable. This stability facilitated unprecedented global trade growth. The monetary chaos that followed the abandonment of the gold standard—hyperinflations in Germany, Zimbabwe, and Venezuela—demonstrates the dangers of unbacked fiat currencies when governments lose discipline.

The Case for Free Banking and Competing Currencies

An alternative to the gold standard is a free banking system wherein private institutions issue their own currencies, competing for customers just as they compete in all other markets. This system, which existed in Scotland during the 18th century and in various American states before the Civil War, would allow market forces to determine which forms of money people prefer to use and hold.

Under free banking, currency issuers would have strong incentives to maintain the value of their notes. If a bank issued currency that depreciated or failed to be redeemed, customers would abandon it for more reliable alternatives. The market would discipline reckless issuers while rewarding those maintaining sound monetary practices. This represents a form of consumer protection far more effective than government regulation.

Competing currencies would allow individuals and businesses to choose money that best suits their needs. Some might prefer stable-valued gold-denominated notes for long-term savings, while others might prefer more liquid but potentially less stable currencies for transactions. This diversity would provide natural hedging against monetary instability.

The innovation that free banking would unleash cannot be predicted in advance. Just as competition in other industries produces unexpected improvements, competition in money would likely generate monetary innovations serving consumer needs in ways that central planning cannot anticipate. The Federal Reserve, by contrast, represents a one-size-fits-all approach to monetary policy that ignores regional, industrial, and individual differences.

Practical Transition Considerations

Critics rightly ask how transition from the current system would work. The practical answer involves a phased approach: first, allowing gold and silver to circulate as legal tender alongside Federal Reserve notes; second, eliminating legal tender laws that force acceptance of fiat currency; third, progressively shrinking Federal Reserve operations as the market develops alternative monetary arrangements.

Sound Treasury management during transition would require the government to live within its means, eliminating deficits and gradually paying down debt. This discipline, while painful initially, would produce a government actually financed by taxation rather than by inflation—a profound improvement in democratic governance.

Banks currently required to hold Federal Reserve reserves could transition to holding gold or operating under clear contractual arrangements with private clearinghouses. The market would develop institutions suited to a sound money environment, as it has developed institutions for every other market need.

Addressing Counterarguments

Mainstream economists raise legitimate concerns about the gold standard and free banking that deserve acknowledgment. They argue that the gold standard contributed to the Great Depression's severity by limiting governments' ability to respond to economic crisis. They note that no major economy has operated under pure free banking in modern times, making predictions about its functioning necessarily speculative. They point to the inconvenience of a money supply tied to gold mining decisions.

These concerns deserve serious engagement. However, they largely assume that central bank interventions actually solve the problems they address. The Great Depression's severity was amplified by Federal Reserve failures to prevent bank runs and provide liquidity. More fundamentally, would a monetary system less prone to artificial booms require as frequent interventions? The counterfactual—a world without the Fed's credit expansions preceding crashes—cannot be tested, but economic theory suggests it might feature smaller but more frequent corrections rather than catastrophic crises.

The speculative nature of free banking predictions cuts both ways. Central banking itself is relatively recent in human history, and its long-term effects remain genuinely unknown. The 2008 crisis and its aftermath, wherein extraordinary Federal Reserve interventions became the new normal, demonstrate that central banking's long-term effects cannot be predicted with confidence either.

Conclusion

The case for ending the Federal Reserve and returning to sound money rests on constitutional principles, economic theory, and historical evidence. While mainstream economists defend central banking, their defense often assumes that alternatives must be perfect to be preferred to the status quo. This asymmetric standard ignores the substantial costs—financial crises, monetary manipulation, erosion of purchasing power—that the current system imposes.

The choice is not between an ideal monetary system and the Federal Reserve, but between an imperfect but market-oriented approach and a centralized system that concentrates enormous power in an unaccountable institution. Given the historical tendency of governments to abuse monetary power, and given the philosophical preference for liberty over control, the burden of proof should fall on central banking's defenders.

The American tradition prizes both economic liberty and limited government. Ending the Federal Reserve would advance both values simultaneously. It would return to the American people the right to choose their own money, discipline the federal government through financial constraint, and trust individuals to manage their own economic affairs without central planning. In a nation founded on distrust of concentrated power, perhaps the greatest argument for ending the Federal Reserve is simply that such power should never have been concentrated in the first place.

The Moral and Economic Imperative to End the Fed: Abolishing Central Banking and Restoring Sound Money

For over a century, the Federal Reserve System has operated as the unelected, unaccountable architect of America's monetary order. Created in 1913 under the guise of stabilizing the economy and preventing financial panics, it has instead presided over the devaluation of the dollar by over 96 percent, engineered the boom-bust cycles it was designed to prevent, and concentrated enormous, unconstitutional power in the hands of a few central planners. The time has come not to reform or audit the Fed, but to abolish it outright—ending the era of fiat currency and restoring a system of sound money through a gold standard or free banking. This is not a radical fringe proposal but a necessary correction to a failed experiment in monetary socialism that has undermined prosperity, liberty, and the moral fabric of economic life.

The Inflation Tax and the Immorality of Fiat Money

The Fed's primary tool—monetary expansion—operates as a hidden and regressive tax on the American people. When the Federal Reserve creates new dollars ex nihilo to finance government deficits or "stimulate" the economy, it does not create wealth; it redistributes it. The first recipients of this new money—large financial institutions, government contractors, and the treasury itself—gain purchasing power before prices adjust. By the time these dollars reach ordinary citizens through wages and savings, prices have risen, and their money's value has been silently confiscated. This "Cantillon Effect" systematically transfers wealth from the poor and middle class to the politically connected financial elite. Such a mechanism is not merely economically destructive; it is morally indefensible. It violates property rights at the most fundamental level, eroding the value of what people have earned and saved through honest labor. A gold standard, by contrast, imposes discipline. Money becomes a claim on a scarce, tangible commodity that cannot be inflated by bureaucratic decree. Under such a system, savings preserve their value, and the silent theft of purchasing power becomes impossible.

Central Banking as the Engine of Economic Instability

Proponents of the Fed claim it smooths the business cycle, yet the evidence reveals the opposite. The Fed manipulates interest rates, the most critical price signals in any economy. When it artificially suppresses rates below what free markets would set, it deceives entrepreneurs and investors. Projects that would be unprofitable under genuine, savings-driven rates appear viable. This misallocation of capital—what Austrian economists call "malinvestment"—creates an illusory boom. But since this boom is not grounded in real savings, it inevitably collapses into bust. The Great Depression, the stagflation of the 1970s, the dot-com bubble, the 2008 financial crisis, and today's inflationary surge all bear the Fed's fingerprints. Each crisis was preceded by periods of artificially cheap credit, and each required ever more dramatic interventions that only sow the seeds for the next disaster. A free banking system, where private banks issue currency backed by specie and are subject to market discipline (including the threat of bank runs), would prevent such systemic manipulation. Interest rates would reflect actual time preferences and savings rates, ensuring that investment aligns with real economic resources.

Concentrated Power and the Corruption of Crony Capitalism

The Fed's monopoly on money creation has created a nexus of corruption between Washington, Wall Street, and the military-industrial complex. The ability to finance deficits through inflation has enabled a century of reckless government growth and warfare without the political accountability of direct taxation. Simultaneously, the doctrine of "too big to fail"—a direct consequence of the Fed's existence—has socialized losses while privatizing gains. When large banks know the Fed will act as a lender of last resort, moral hazard explodes. They take outsized risks, comfortable in the knowledge that their failures will be bailed out through Fed-conjured dollars, while smaller, more prudent competitors are left to fail. This is not capitalism; it is monetary socialism for the rich. Ending the Fed would demolish this corrupt edifice. Without a central bank to backstop their failures, financial institutions would be forced to operate responsibly or face market extinction. The intimate link between government deficit spending and monetary debasement would be severed, restoring fiscal discipline.

The Constitutional and Historical Case

The U.S. Constitution grants Congress the power to "coin Money" and "regulate the Value thereof," but this was never understood by the Framers as a power to emit paper fiat or charter a central bank. The Tenth Amendment reserves all powers not explicitly granted to the federal government to the states and the people—nowhere does the Constitution sanction a monopoly currency issuer like the Fed. Historically, America thrived under competitive currencies and metallic standards. The classical gold standard (1834-1913, with interruptions) oversaw the most dramatic rise in living standards and industrial output in human history, all with relatively stable prices. The Fed's creation in 1913 marked a turning point from monetary stability toward perpetual inflation and crisis. The claim that we "need" a central bank is ahistorical; it confuses necessity with the self-serving narratives of those who benefit from its existence.

The Path Forward: Gold and Free Competition

Abolishing the Fed requires a clear alternative. First, the U.S. must legalize competing currencies. Private banks and financial institutions should be free to issue their own notes, fully redeemable in gold or silver, and let the market determine which currencies are most reliable. Gresham's Law ("bad money drives out good") only applies when legal tender laws force acceptance of depreciating fiat; in a truly free market, sound money would drive out bad. Second, the federal government should return to a gold standard, not by fixing an arbitrary price, but by defining the dollar as a specific weight of gold and allowing convertibility. This would restore confidence, end inflation, and force government to live within its means. The transition would be challenging, but the alternative—continuing down the path of currency debasement—is national suicide.

Conclusion: Liberty Requires Sound Money

The Federal Reserve is an institution incompatible with a free society. Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of abolishing the Federal Reserve, ending central banking and fiat currency, and returning to a gold standard or a free banking system that allows competing private currencies.
Model Response:

A monetary system built on a coercive central bank and unconstrained fiat currency is inherently unstable, unjust, and incompatible with a free society. The Federal Reserve should be abolished, central banking ended, and money returned to either a gold-based standard or a genuine free banking regime in which private currencies compete.

This isn’t nostalgia or ideology alone; it follows from economic logic, historical experience, and basic principles of individual liberty.

I. Central banking and fiat money: central planning by another name

The Federal Reserve is often portrayed as a neutral “technocratic” institution managing the economy for the public good. In reality, it is a central planner of the single most important price in the economy: the interest rate, as well as the quantity of money itself.

That means it faces the same core problem that plagues all central planning: the knowledge problem. No committee—no matter how credentialed—can possibly know the “correct” interest rate, the “right” amount of credit, or the “appropriate” level of inflation for a vast, complex economy of hundreds of millions of individuals making billions of daily decisions.

When the Fed sets rates artificially low or floods the system with money, it distorts price signals:

  • Mispricing of risk: Investors underprice risk because cheap money makes almost any project appear profitable on paper.
  • Malinvestment: Businesses, governments, and households are incentivized to borrow excessively for projects that only make sense under artificially easy monetary conditions.
  • Asset bubbles: Capital flows disproportionately into real estate, equities, and speculative assets, inflating bubbles that eventually burst.

This is not a side-effect; it is built into the logic of discretionary central banking. By manipulating the money supply and suppressing interest rates, the Fed systematically causes boom‑and‑bust cycles. The boom feels good and is politically convenient; the bust is blamed on “market failure” rather than the central bank that set the stage.

Moreover, fiat money—unbacked paper currency declared legal tender by the state—allows the central bank and government to finance themselves by stealth taxation: inflation.

  • New money enters the economy through specific channels first (banks, government contractors, financial markets), benefiting those closest to the source.
  • Ordinary savers, wage earners, and those on fixed incomes see their purchasing power eroded over time.
  • This “Cantillon effect” amounts to a hidden redistribution of wealth from the public to the politically connected.

Fiat money thus combines economic instability with moral and political corruption. It is a tool of silent expropriation.

II. The Federal Reserve’s track record: failure by its own standards

The Fed was created in 1913 to stop financial panics, stabilize prices, and reduce volatility. Judged against those goals, its record is dismal.

  1. The Great Depression (1929–1930s)
    The worst economic collapse in American history occurred under the Federal Reserve’s watch. Its prior credit expansion fueled the 1920s boom; its policies during the early 1930s turned a severe downturn into a catastrophe. Even mainstream economic historians (e.g., Friedman and Schwartz) attribute a large share of the blame to the Fed.

  2. The Great Inflation (1960s–1970s)
    After abandoning any real tie to gold, the Fed presided over a decade-plus of high and unstable inflation, eroding savings and undermining the dollar’s integrity. This ended only with painful interest rate hikes and a deep recession in the early 1980s.

  3. The Dot‑Com and Housing Bubbles (1990s–2000s)
    The Fed’s low interest rate policy in the early 2000s, after the dot‑com crash, helped fuel the massive housing bubble. The subsequent collapse in 2008 triggered a global financial crisis—again blamed on “market excess,” even though the cheap credit that fed it was centrally engineered.

  4. Post‑2008 and COVID era
    Zero interest rates and Quantitative Easing created a world where:

    • Asset prices soared far beyond fundamentals.
    • Savers were punished, and speculation was rewarded.
    • Government debt exploded, cushioned by the Fed’s willingness to monetize it. The unprecedented monetary expansion during and after COVID further entrenched inflation and widened wealth inequality.

Far from “smoothing” the business cycle, the Fed has amplified and synchronized financial crises. Instead of providing stability, it has socialized risk, encouraged leverage, and entrenched “too big to fail” institutions—all under a regime of fiat money that steadily erodes the dollar’s purchasing power.

III. The case for sound money: gold as a monetary anchor

Gold is not perfect, but it is vastly superior to politically managed paper. For centuries—and across cultures—gold emerged on the market as money precisely because it has key properties:

  • Scarce and impossible to print at will.
  • Durable and not consumed in use.
  • Divisible and uniform, allowing small and large transactions.
  • Globally recognized and easily transportable in high value‑to‑weight form.

Under a classical gold standard, money supply growth is constrained by the cost and feasibility of mining. No committee can simply decide to double the money supply to bail out financial markets or to smooth over fiscal irresponsibility.

Economic benefits of a gold standard

  1. Long‑run price stability
    Under the classical gold standard (roughly 1870–1914), many countries experienced long-term price stability, with mild periods of inflation and deflation balancing out over decades. Savers could plan for the future without fearing systematic currency debasement.

  2. Fiscal discipline
    Governments constrained by redeemable gold‑backed money cannot indefinitely finance deficits with the printing press. Large wars and expansive welfare states become more visibly expensive and politically accountable, because they must be financed by taxation or genuine borrowing, not hidden inflation.

  3. Limiting credit booms
    Banks cannot expand credit without limit when they must redeem liabilities in gold on demand. Over‑issuance risks runs and insolvency. This imposes a market discipline on credit creation absent in fiat systems where central banks act as unconditional lenders of last resort.

  4. International stability
    A gold‑based system operates as a kind of automatic international balance of payments mechanism. Trade imbalances trigger gold flows that incentivize policy adjustments, rather than allowing endless accumulation of imbalances funded by central bank swaps and debt.

The usual criticism—that a gold standard is “a barbarous relic” that cannot support modern growth—is historically ignorant. The 19th century, under a largely gold‑based international system, saw the fastest sustained growth in living standards the world had seen up to that time.

IV. Beyond gold: free banking and competing private currencies

A gold standard is one way to constrain money; another is to abolish the monetary monopoly entirely and allow free banking: competing private institutions issuing their own currencies and deposits, redeemable in a base asset (which could be gold, or another widely accepted store of value).

Under free banking:

  • Banks issue notes and deposits, redeemable on demand.
  • Badly run banks lose customers and face runs; well‑run banks win trust.
  • Clearinghouses and interbank arrangements discipline over‑issuance, because any bank that expands too aggressively faces adverse clearings—other banks present its notes for redemption.

This isn’t a utopian theory; it has historical precedent:

  • Scotland (18th–19th centuries): A largely free banking system functioned with remarkable stability, low failure rates, and limited government interference.
  • Canada (pre‑1935): Also experienced fewer and milder banking crises than the more regulated and fragmented U.S. system.
  • Suffolk System in New England (19th century): A private clearinghouse effectively regulated the banking system, disciplining risky issuers.

A modern free banking regime could include:

  • Gold‑backed currencies.
  • Commodity‑backed claims.
  • Private digital currencies, including cryptographic ones.
  • Market‑chosen stable units of account.

Instead of a single monopolistic money managed by a political institution, individuals and businesses would choose among competing providers based on trust, convenience, and stability. Fraud and breach of contract would remain illegal, but the structure of money and banking would be decided by market competition rather than by law.

V. Answering common objections

1. “Without the Fed, crises would be worse.”

Historically, many financial panics in the U.S. were caused or worsened by government interventions (unit banking laws, legal restrictions on note issuance, suspension of specie payments) rather than by the absence of a central bank. In contrast, freer systems (like Scotland’s and Canada’s) were more stable without a central bank.

Moreover, the Fed’s role as lender of last resort creates moral hazard: banks can take on more risk, knowing they’ll be rescued. That is not “stability”; it’s institutionalized recklessness.

2. “A gold standard or free banking would be deflationary and harmful.”

Not all deflation is the same. There is a crucial difference between:

  • Benign deflation: Prices gradually fall because productivity rises (goods become cheaper to produce). This is natural and beneficial; consumers get more for less.
  • Monetary deflation: Abrupt contractions of the money supply due to banking collapse, often triggered or mismanaged by central banks themselves.

Under a well-run gold or free banking system, mild deflation from productivity gains is normal and healthy. The fear of deflation has been exaggerated to justify perpetual inflation, which benefits debtors and governments at the expense of savers and wage earners.

3. “Modern economies need discretionary monetary policy.”

This assumes that a small committee of central bankers can and should “fine-tune” the economy. But empirical evidence shows that such discretion often amplifies cycles. Stable rules—or better, a competitive system where rules emerge from market discipline—are superior to politicized improvisation.

If discretionary policy were so beneficial, we would expect a monotonic decline in crises and volatility under the Fed. We have not seen that.

4. “Free banking would be chaotic.”

Markets handle complexity far better than centralized bureaucracy. The payment systems, credit markets, and derivatives of today are already highly complex—yet they function largely due to private innovation. Where we see catastrophic failures, they often stem from distorted incentives created by regulation and central bank backstops, not from competition itself.

Chaos is what we already have: serial bubbles, mass bailouts, and creeping inflation under a single monetary authority whose failures are socialized.

VI. Practical steps toward abolishing the Fed and restoring monetary freedom

Transition matters, and sudden overnight abolition of the Federal Reserve without preparation would be disruptive. But a deliberate path is possible:

  1. End legal tender laws
    Allow contracts and payments in any mutually agreed medium—gold, silver, private digital currencies, foreign currencies, etc. Remove the dollar’s legal monopoly status.

  2. Remove barriers to private currency issuance
    Legalize and deregulate (within general fraud and solvency laws) private currency providers, gold‑backed banks, and alternative payment systems.

  3. Phase out Fed support for government deficits
    Prohibit the Fed from purchasing newly issued government debt. Force fiscal discipline by requiring the government to finance itself through taxation or borrowing at market rates.

  4. Convertibility and reserves
    Gradually introduce redeemability of dollars for a commodity (such as gold) at a defined rate, or allow banks to issue redeemable notes while the legacy fiat system competes alongside them.

  5. Wind down the Fed’s functions

    • Privatize or decentralize payment and settlement systems.
    • Transfer necessary statistical roles to independent agencies.
    • Remove the Fed’s regulatory privileges; bank supervision can be handled by a combination of general corporate law, market rating agencies, and specialized institutions, as in other industries.

  6. Constitutional or legal restraints
    Lock in a prohibition on central banking and fiat money financing to prevent future re‑creation of a monetary monopoly.

VII. Why abolition matters: liberty, justice, and prosperity

Central banking and fiat currency are not neutral technical choices; they structure society’s incentives and power relationships.

  • They empower governments to wage larger wars and build larger bureaucracies than taxpayers would willingly fund.
  • They reward debtors over savers, speculation over prudence, and political access over productive enterprise.
  • They repeatedly redistribute wealth through inflation and asset booms and busts, harming the least politically connected.

A gold standard or free banking with competing private currencies would:

  • Restore honest money whose value cannot be manipulated at will.
  • Align banking and credit with market discipline rather than political favor.
  • Limit the size and scope of government by removing the inflationary backstop.
  • Allow citizens to choose their money, rather than being forced into a single politicized currency.

The Federal Reserve and central banking more broadly are 20th‑century experiments that have failed on their own terms. Abolishing the Fed, ending fiat money, and moving toward a gold‑anchored or genuinely competitive monetary order is not regression; it is a necessary step toward a more stable, free, and just economic system.

From the perspective of people who see central banking and fiat money as inherently inflationary and harmful (often influenced by Austrian economics, some libertarian thought, and “sound money” advocates), the case for abolishing the Federal Reserve, ending fiat money, and moving to gold or currency competition rests on a few core claims:

  • Under a fiat system, money is not backed by a physical commodity; it’s created by:

    • Commercial banks via fractional-reserve lending.
  • To these critics, this means:
    • There is no hard constraint on money creation.
    • Political and financial interests have strong incentives to keep expanding the money supply.

1.2. Inflation as “hidden taxation”

  • They see chronic inflation as:
    • A stealth tax on cash holders and savers: newly created money reduces the purchasing power of existing money.
    • A way for governments to finance deficits without openly raising taxes or borrowing at market rates.
  • From this view:
    • Citizens who save in cash or fixed-income assets are quietly expropriated.
    • Responsible behavior (saving) gets punished while debtors and spenders are rewarded.

1.3. Central banking distorts interest rates and causes boom–bust cycles

  • They argue that the Fed:
    • Artificially suppresses interest rates below the “natural” market rate.
    • Encourages excessive borrowing, speculation, and malinvestment (e.g., housing bubble, tech bubbles).
  • This is the Austrian business cycle story:
    1. Easy money and low rates → credit boom → investments that only look profitable under cheap credit.
    2. Reality reasserts itself → projects fail → bust, recession, and financial crisis.
  • In this view, the Fed:
    • Does not stabilize the economy; it creates larger and more damaging cycles than a free market would.

2. Reasons and supposed benefits of abolishing the Federal Reserve

2.1. Ending the monopoly on money

  • The Fed is seen as a government-granted monopoly over currency and base money.
  • Abolition is supposed to:
    • End the privileged position of one institution controlling the money supply and interest rates.
    • Allow money to emerge from market processes and competition, not central planning.

2.2. Removing political manipulation of money

Supporters argue the Fed is inevitably political, even if formally “independent”:

  • Politicians want:
    • Low interest rates and easy money before elections.
    • Cheap financing for wars and welfare programs.
  • Abolishing the Fed would:
    • Make it harder for governments to “buy” political support with monetary policy.
    • Force more honest, transparent budgeting and taxation.

2.3. Reducing or eliminating the “inflation tax”

  • Without a central bank:
    • The government cannot easily monetize its debt—i.e., turn deficits into new money.
  • Advocates expect:
    • Lower and more stable prices over the long run.
    • Better protection of savings, pensions, and wages from gradual erosion.

2.4. Less moral hazard in the financial system

  • The Fed is seen as:
    • The ultimate backstop for banks and financial firms (lender of last resort, bailouts, “too big to fail”).
  • Abolishing it is supposed to:
    • Remove guarantees that encourage reckless risk-taking.
    • Force banks to be more conservative, maintain higher capital, and manage risk properly, because failure would be real and final.

2.5. Business cycles would be fewer and milder

  • In the Austrian view:
    • Without a central bank pushing rates artificially low and expanding credit, credit booms would be limited.
    • Recessions would still occur but would be:
      • Localized to specific errors.
      • Shorter and less severe, because they wouldn’t follow massive, economy-wide credit distortions.

3. Reasons and supposed benefits of eliminating fiat money

3.1. Restoring a “hard constraint” on money creation

  • Under fiat money:
    • The supply of money is essentially bounded only by political will and institutional constraints.
  • Eliminating fiat money and tying money to a commodity (like gold) or other strict rule supposedly:
    • Prevents arbitrary expansion.
    • Forces discipline on both governments and banks.

3.2. Protecting savings and long-term planning

  • Advocates argue:
    • People can better plan for decades if the value of money is stable or gently deflationary.
    • Under sound money, money gains purchasing power over time, rewarding thrift.
  • This is supposed to:
    • Encourage long-term investment financed by real savings, rather than cheap credit.
    • Improve capital allocation and productivity.

3.3. Moral and property-rights arguments

  • Many see fiat inflation as a moral issue:
    • You worked for your money; inflation reduces its value without your consent.
  • Abandoning fiat is seen as:
    • Respecting property rights in people’s savings.
    • Ending a system where states can quietly dilute private wealth.

4. Reasons and supposed benefits of a gold standard

Supporters are not all identical, but typical claims include:

4.1. Historical track record of long-run price stability

  • Under classical gold standards (e.g., 19th–early 20th century), they point out:
    • Over long stretches, prices were relatively stable or mildly deflationary.
    • Periods of war inflation were often followed by deflation back to pre-war price levels.
  • They argue this is superior to the persistent upward trend in prices under modern fiat systems.

4.2. Automatic discipline on governments and banks

  • Gold limits:
    • How much money can be created; it must be backed by gold reserves (depending on the arrangement).
    • Governments’ ability to finance large, continuous deficits.
  • Supposed benefits:
    • Smaller and more limited governments, because:
      • War and welfare spending must be financed by explicit taxation or honest borrowing.
    • Banks must maintain redemption discipline: issue notes and deposits only to the extent they can meet gold convertibility.

4.3. International stability and fewer currency crises

  • Under a gold standard:
    • Exchange rates between countries on gold are fixed (in terms of gold content).
    • Trade imbalances are corrected via gold flows and price adjustments (the “price–specie flow mechanism”).
  • Advocates say this:
    • Reduces currency wars, beggar-thy-neighbor devaluations, and competitive printing.
    • Creates a predictable international environment for trade and investment.

4.4. Predictability and certainty

  • A gold standard is seen as:
    • A rules-based system rather than discretionary.
    • Easy to understand: money is defined as a certain weight of gold.
  • Supposed advantages:
    • Investors, businesses, and workers can make long-term contracts and investments with confidence that the unit of account won’t be manipulated at will.

5. Reasons and supposed benefits of a free market in currencies (free banking / currency competition)

Some critics of central banking prefer not just gold, but competition among different forms of money.

5.1. No legal-tender monopoly

  • Today, the state typically:
    • Declares its currency legal tender.
    • Taxes and regulations entrench its use and make alternatives costly or impractical.
  • A free market in currencies would:
    • Remove legal obstacles to private money issuance and use.
    • Allow people to choose which money they trust—gold-backed notes, silver, stablecoins, cryptocurrencies, etc.

5.2. Competition as a check on inflation and mismanagement

  • The key claim:
    • If one issuer inflates too much or mismanages its currency:
      • People can shift to another currency.
  • So competition should:
    • Discipline issuers to maintain stable value and sound banking practices.
    • Perform the same role competition plays in other markets—punish bad actors and reward prudent ones.

5.3. Market-selected money and banking structures

  • Instead of government dictating the monetary standard:
    • People would gravitate to whatever money best meets their needs (durable, divisible, stable in value, widely accepted).
  • Historically, proponents argue:
    • Commodity money and private note issuance (free banking systems in Scotland, Canada, etc.) worked reasonably well where they were allowed.
  • Supposed benefits:
    • Innovation in financial contracts and payment systems.
    • Better matching of money types to different uses (e.g., very stable store-of-value currencies vs. fast, cheap, transaction-oriented ones).

5.4. Risk is priced, not socialized

  • In a free banking world:
    • No central bank guarantees, no government deposit insurance by default.
    • Banks must attract customers with safety, transparency, and good management.
  • Result, according to advocates:
    • Safer banks overall because depositors and investors monitor risk.
    • Failure is possible but localized; no systemic “everything-or-nothing” central bank rescue.

6. Summary of the supposed overall benefits (from this perspective)

People who oppose central banking and fiat money believe that:

  • Abolishing the Fed would:

    • End the monopoly over money and interest rates.
    • Remove a key driver of inflation, moral hazard, and boom–bust cycles.

  • Eliminating fiat money would:

    • Stop governments and banks from diluting purchasing power at will.
    • Protect savers and encourage long-term, real-savings-based investment.

  • Adopting a gold standard would:

    • Provide long-run price stability and international monetary order.
    • Force fiscal discipline and limit the growth of government.

  • Allowing a free market in currencies would:

    • Harness competition to keep money honest and well-managed.
    • Let individuals choose the money they trust, rather than being forced into a state monopoly.

Mainstream economists and policymakers contest many of these claims, but this is, in condensed form, how critics of central banking and fiat money understand the problem and the benefits they expect from a gold standard or currency competition.

“They just don’t understand modern economics. They think numbers should add up, debts should be repayable, and money should hold value over time. It’s cute, honestly. Like grown adults believing in responsibility.”

My friends,

There is a quiet tragedy in our time that most people never see.

They feel it, but they do not see it.

They feel it in the rising cost of food and rent.
They feel it in the shrinking power of their paychecks.
They feel it when they save for years, only to discover that the dollar itself has been quietly draining away in value.

This tragedy is not an accident of history or an inevitability of markets.
It is the direct result of a conscious political decision:
to give a small committee of unelected technocrats control over our money, and to sever that money from any real anchor in the physical world.

I am speaking, of course, about the Federal Reserve System and our regime of fiat currency.

The Core Problem: Power Without Accountability

In the United States, we pride ourselves on checks and balances.
We distrust concentrated power in the hands of a few.
We do not allow a king, a dictator, or a single party to control our lives.

And yet, we tolerate an institution that can:

  • Create money out of nothing.
  • Decide the price of borrowing for every business, every homeowner, every student.
  • Bail out its favorites and let others fail.
  • Pick winners and losers across the entire economy…

…without ever facing a real election, without real market discipline, and largely insulated from the people whose lives it reshapes.

That institution is the Federal Reserve.

The Fed sets interest rates, manipulates the money supply, and attempts to “manage” the economy as though it were a machine, not a complex web of free choices by millions of individuals.

It claims to smooth out the business cycle.
It claims to preserve purchasing power.
It claims to be a neutral steward.

Look around you and judge for yourself.

  • The dollar has lost the vast majority of its purchasing power since the Fed’s creation in 1913.
  • The boom-and-bust cycles have not vanished; they have been amplified by waves of easy money followed by crushing contractions.
  • Asset bubbles—housing, stocks, bonds—have become recurring features of our economy, fueled in no small part by artificially cheap credit.

The very institution that claims to stabilize the economy has become one of the greatest sources of instability.

Fiat Money: A Promise Without Discipline

Our money today is “fiat” money.
It is not redeemable for gold or silver or any tangible asset.
It is backed by nothing but confidence—and ultimately, by the power of the government to tax and to compel.

That means when the government wants to spend beyond its means, it does not need to raise taxes openly and face the fury of the voter. It can borrow, and when the borrowing becomes too heavy, the Federal Reserve can step in and buy that debt with newly created dollars.

It is taxation by stealth.
It is a quiet expropriation of savers and workers through inflation.

Who pays?

  • The worker on a fixed salary whose wages do not keep up with rising prices.
  • The retiree who saved in dollars, only to see the value of those savings erode.
  • The poor, who hold cash, not stocks and real estate, and watch as the cost of living outpaces their ability to adapt.

Who benefits?

  • Those closest to the source of new money: large financial institutions, the government itself, and those who are politically connected.
  • Those who can borrow at near-zero interest while everyone else struggles under the distorted price signals that the Fed has imposed.

This is not a free market.
This is not sound money.
This is a system in which the state enjoys a monopoly over money and credit, and uses that monopoly to shift wealth, pick winners and losers, and fund its own ambitions.

Sound Money: Gold Standard and Free Banking

We do not have to accept this.

There are alternatives—tested in history, grounded in economic reality, and aligned with the principles of liberty.

1. A Gold Standard

Under a gold standard, the currency is simply a claim on a defined weight of gold. The government does not conjure money out of thin air; it must respect real constraints.

  • The supply of money cannot be expanded at will to fund endless wars, bailouts, or political promises.
  • Savings retain their value over time because money is anchored to a scarce, tangible asset.
  • Long-term planning becomes possible when people can trust the value of their money decades into the future.

Historically, the classical gold standard of the 19th century coincided with extraordinary growth, industrial expansion, and long-run price stability. While it was imperfect and often undermined by governments themselves, it embodied a crucial idea: that money should be a neutral medium of exchange, not a political tool.

2. Free Banking and Monetary Competition

An even more radical—and in many ways more consistent—approach is free banking:
letting banks, institutions, or even private entities issue their own currencies, backed by assets they choose, subject to market discipline and competition.

You, the individual, would decide which money to hold.

  • If a bank over-issues its currency and undermines its value, people will abandon it.
  • If an issuer offers sound money backed by reliable reserves—gold, commodities, or other robust assets—people will flock to it.
  • Exchange rates between different monies would reflect the market’s judgment of their quality.

In such a system, no single institution would have a monopoly over money. Money would become what it should have always been: a service provided in a free market, with competition, transparency, and the possibility of failure for those who mismanage it.

This is how we get real accountability—not from congressional hearings years after a crisis, but from the daily choices of millions of individuals.

Economic Freedom and Moral Responsibility

This is not just an economic question. It is a moral one.

When the state controls money, it controls the lifeblood of the economy. It gains a powerful lever over every contract, every savings account, every retirement plan, every business.

The more power it has over money, the more temptation there is to abuse that power:

  • To fund deficits without limit.
  • To paper over structural problems with cheap credit.
  • To reward those who are politically close and punish those who are not.

A system of sound money—whether through a gold standard, free banking, or a combination—forces honesty.

Governments must tax openly or borrow honestly.
They cannot rely on a central bank to silently dilute the currency whenever reality catches up with them.

Honest money is the economic foundation of a free society.
You cannot have truly limited government with unlimited money creation.
You cannot have long-term prosperity on a foundation of short-term manipulation.

Answering the Objections

We are told:

  • “Without the Fed, the economy will be chaotic.”
  • “Without fiat money, we cannot respond to crises.”
  • “Without centralized control, everything will collapse.”

But look at what centralized control has already given us:

  • The Great Depression, deepened by monetary mistakes.
  • The stagflation of the 1970s.
  • The tech bubble of the late 1990s.
  • The housing bubble and the crash of 2008.
  • The unprecedented expansion of the Fed’s balance sheet and the distortion of interest rates in the last decade.
  • Surging asset prices alongside growing inequality and chronic anxiety about the cost of living.

Central planners at the Fed do not possess perfect knowledge.
They do not see the vast, intricate, constantly changing information that is contained in real market prices and interest rates set by genuine supply and demand.

They are guessing—guessing with enormous consequences.

By contrast, a system of sound money and free banking does not rely on the wisdom of a committee. It relies on the incentives and information embedded in millions of voluntary transactions.

That is not chaos. That is order—emergent order, the kind that has built civilization itself.

The Path Forward: From Monopoly to Freedom

Abolishing the Federal Reserve and ending the fiat money regime will not be simple. It will require courage, careful planning, and a transition that minimizes disruption.

But the first step is intellectual and moral: we must stop treating the current system as sacred and unchangeable.

  • We must allow competing forms of money—gold-backed currencies, private digital currencies, and other alternatives—to operate freely without punitive taxation or regulation designed to protect the monopoly of fiat.
  • We must gradually reduce and then end the Fed’s role in setting interest rates, letting markets determine the price of credit.
  • We must move toward a framework in which money is anchored to something real, in which its supply cannot be expanded at the whim of politicians or central bankers.

The end goal is clear:
No single institution should have the power to debase your savings, distort the price of credit, or socialize losses while privatizing gains.

A Call to Courage

The fight over money is not a technical dispute reserved for economists. It is a struggle over who controls the future.

Do we trust free people to choose their own money, to save, to invest, to plan, to build?
Or do we entrust our economic destiny to a boardroom in Washington, D.C.?

Do we want a dollar that reflects political expediency and short-term calculations?
Or a form of money that respects time, effort, and real value?

A society that wants to be free must demand honest money.
A people who wish to stand on their own feet must reject the quiet tyranny of inflation and the hidden hand of monetary manipulation.

So let us say, clearly and without apology:

  • End the Fed’s monopoly on money.
  • End the era of unbacked fiat currency.
  • Restore sound money—through a gold standard, through free banking, through real competition and real discipline.

We owe it to the saver, to the worker, to the entrepreneur.
We owe it to future generations who deserve a world where money is not a rigged game, but a trustworthy tool.
We owe it to the very idea of liberty.

It is time to take back our money.
It is time to take back our future.

The Federal Reserve embodies the fatal conceit that a small committee of central planners can effectively manage the money supply for a $25 trillion economy. The Federal Reserve's policies have become the primary driver of wealth inequality in America. Through its zero-interest-rate policies and quantitative easing programs, the Fed has inflated asset bubbles that benefit the wealthy while crushing middle-class savers. When the Fed prints trillions of dollars to purchase government bonds and mortgage-backed securities, it artificially inflates stock prices and real estate values, enriching asset owners while pricing younger generations out of homeownership.

The Cantillon Effect—whereby those who receive new money first benefit at the expense of those who receive it last—operates as a massive wealth transfer mechanism from Main Street to Wall Street. Investment banks borrow at near-zero rates from the Fed's discount window, then lend to ordinary Americans at credit card rates exceeding 20%. This is not free-market capitalism; it is a rigged system of monetary socialism for the elite.

The Fed's manipulation of interest rates creates artificial booms that inevitably end in devastating busts. By suppressing interest rates below their natural market levels, the Fed sends false signals to entrepreneurs and investors, encouraging malinvestment in unsustainable projects. History demonstrates that economies thrive under monetary systems based on real value rather than government fiat. When the dollar was redeemable for a set amount of gold, individuals and businesses alike used an asset with intrinsic worth. One of the most pivotal arguments against a central bank is that it enables government to spend beyond its means without immediate consequences. With the ability to “print” money—digitally or physically—the government can finance projects, wars, and social programs without directly raising taxes. This relative ease of financing often delays political accountability. By contrast, a gold standard or competing private currencies would severely limit the government’s ability to inflate itself out of debt or fund its operations without direct consent (through taxation or public debt offerings) from constituents and investors.

Inflation hits savers and lower-income earners hardest by reducing the purchasing power of the dollar. Those with wealth in real assets like property, equities, or gold can hedge against inflation. Meanwhile, wage earners often see their incomes lag behind the general rise in prices. This wealth transfer effect typifies one of the core criticisms of the Federal Reserve’s ability to shape monetary policy. A currency bound to a commodity or developed in a competitive market—where individual issuers face consequences for devaluing their notes—would presumably keep inflation in check and protect the real value of workers’ earnings and retirements.

  1. Encouraging Saving, Investment, and Financial Responsibility

Critics of central banking contend that artificially low interest rates foster irresponsible borrowing and risk-taking. When the Federal Reserve keeps rates near zero, it can motivate corporations and consumers to borrow excessively, which can fuel asset bubbles and distort business investment decisions. Under a true gold standard or a free banking system where competing currencies must maintain public trust by backing their notes with tangible reserves, interest rates would be determined by real market demand for liquidity and credit—rather than by policymakers.

A monetary system driven by genuine supply and demand for savings should, in theory, reward responsible lenders and borrowers alike. It tests entrepreneurial ventures on their merits rather than their ability to access cheap credit. This discipline can reduce the frequency and severity of financial bubbles.   1. Promoting Competition and Innovation in Monetary Services

In a free banking framework, private entities could issue currencies backed by gold, silver, or other commodities.   1. Recalibrating the Role of Government and Financial Institutions

A gold standard or free banking system pushes for a recalibration of government and financial institutions toward more transparent, limited roles. Advocates, however, see a future of sound money anchored by tangible assets, free from centralized manipulation, and bolstered by real-world market discipline. Whether through a gold standard or free competition in currencies, proponents argue that breaking free from the central bank’s monopoly can rejuvenate trust in the financial system. For over a century, the United States has operated under an economic experiment unprecedented in human history: a state-managed fiat currency system anchored by a central bank. Furthermore, fiat currency functions as a hidden, regressive tax. This inflation does not harm the well-connected evenly; it first enriches those closest to the monetary spigot—large banks, hedge funds, and government contractors—while punishing wage earners and savers. The working class sees their cost of living rise relentlessly, while their savings accounts yield near-zero returns. As economist Henry Hazlitt argued, inflation is a form of legalized counterfeiting that transfers wealth from the productive sectors of society to the politically favored.

To end this cycle of theft and instability, we must dismantle the Federal Reserve and replace it with a system rooted in property rights and market competition. Two primary pathways exist: a strict commodity standard, such as gold, or a system of free banking.

A return to a gold standard would reintroduce an objective discipline to the monetary system. Gold cannot be printed by executive order or conjured via computer keystrokes by central bankers. Its supply is limited by the actual costs of mining, ensuring that the currency retains its purchasing power over long horizons. Under a gold standard, governments are forced to live within their means, as they cannot simply print money to fund endless wars and bloated bureaucracies.
